title: How To Manage Whole-Class Behavior While Working With A Small Group -working-with-a-small-group/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin addresses the frustration of trying to run small-group instruction while the rest of the class interrupts, misbehaves, or demands attention. He argues teachers shouldn't look for quick-fix techniques for each disruption but instead trace the problem to its root cause: students are unprepared to work independently. The solution is to build strong, precise whole-class lessons with clear, visible expectations, checked understanding, and guided practice before ever releasing students to independent work while pulling small groups. He warns that shifting full responsibility for learning onto students, and weaning them off constant teacher availability, can take three to four weeks for classes with deep learned helplessness. Once students prove they can work independently under observation, teachers can pull small groups without constant interruption, periodically glancing up to verify all is well.
points: Chronic interruptions during small-group time stem from a root cause: students aren't yet prepared to work independently.
Effective classroom management addresses root causes rather than applying situational quick fixes to each disruption.
Whole-class lessons before independent work must be vibrant, precise, and paired with checked understanding and guided practice.
Weaning students off constant teacher availability can take three to four weeks for classes with deep learned helplessness.
Once independence is proven, teachers can focus fully on small-group instruction with only occasional visual checks.

In this case, the students outside the small group are misbehaving because they’re unprepared to work independently, and thus don’t do it well.
Your class must first prove that they can work on their own—under your observing eye—for at least the length of time you wish to meet with small groups.
You have to show them through directed teaching and modeling that once the lesson has been taught, the responsibility for learning shifts in total from you to them.

It’s okay and a good idea to periodically peek up from your small group to make sure all is well.
